issues.explanation: The gate does two jobs. It allows at most one start per cooldown period for each repository and operation pair. With hold=True, it also refuses a second start while the first is still running. It has no burst allowance, no counts of refused requests, and no limit shared across server processes. So it matches only part of the catalogue's Rate Limiter. The conformance score of 65 already reflects this, but presence='present' could make it sound complete.

value_json.summary: The assessment is accurate and well supported. The supplied code includes all of api_operation_gate.py, and it confirms each local claim. The clock is read before the lock is taken. Cooldown values are never checked. A first start falls back to a last-start time of 0.0. A NaN or negative cooldown lets every request through. A refusal for work that is already running returns the cooldown as the wait time, but that time does not tell when the work will finish. The recommendation to improve the existing gate, rather than add limits elsewhere, fits the evidence: no request-rate measurements or caller code are supplied. The issues below are minor wording and labelling points. None of them changes the result.

issues.explanation: The HistoryImportCancelled docstring says it is raised "between atomic frames". This means the authors expect each frame to save fully or not at all. Yet in materialize_revision, the reused-frame branch calls rebase_existing_snapshot, which has its own transaction. Then it calls refresh_historical_snapshot_intelligence separately. If the second step fails, the rebase stays saved, but state.baseline_snapshot_id does not advance. The assessment's placement points at this spot without citing the stated expectation.

value_json.summary: The assessment holds up. A Unit of Work is one object that collects related database changes and saves them all at once or not at all. The repository already uses short database transactions for history frames. The evidence does not show a need for a shared object that tracks changes. Keeping the current design is the right call, as long as someone checks how reused history frames are saved. One supporting fact was missed: a history.py comment calls frames "atomic", meaning each frame should save fully or not at all. The reused-frame path saves in two separate steps. That makes the suggested check more pointed, but it does not change the recommendation.

design.control_model: Each request runs once from start to end: entry point, gate, then either a store read or a snapshot read, analysis, and a checked write. design.failure_isolation: An analysis that crashes writes no record, so the latest good record stays in place. Two writers at once cause a conflict error, not a mixed record. A failed restore leaves the current settings as they were, because the backup is checked before anything is changed.

Passing release checks or benchmarks does not prove that a live deployment works.

relationships.rationale: Every way in passes the same checks, so all of them refuse requests for the same reasons.

Read requests fetch existing records without running analysis.
Every record is checked against today's files before anyone sees it.

The current-or-out-of-date label is attached before any cutting.
Entry points only format and send. They do not decide what to cut.
Only setup changes which repositories and profiles are allowed.
Moved records enter and leave through the store, so the store stays the single owner.
The CLI starts setup, dry runs, and restores.

design.state_ownership: Three kinds of saved data, each with one owner. Targets and profiles belong to the target list and change only through setup. Analysis records belong to the record store and are never edited. Backups belong to the setup tool. The engine, shaper, freshness checker, and entry points save nothing between requests.
design.summary: One store keeps every analysis result as a record that is never edited after it is written. Each record carries a fingerprint, which is a hash of the repository files it read. The analysis step only reads a repository and returns a new record. It never writes anything itself. Every way in (CLI, HTTP API, MCP tools, browser dashboard) only reads records or asks for new ones. None of them keeps its own copy of results. Freshness means one check: does the record's fingerprint still match the files on disk today?

General reliability and speed promises.
How large repositories can get before hashing on every read becomes too slow.

Their startup and communication costs buy that isolation. Capture failure prevents analysis from claiming stable inputs. A save failure stops further progress for the affected request; a shared store failure stops new work. Formatting failure leaves saved analysis available. The single controller and store remain shared failure points.
information_flows: Requests carry target selection, analysis settings, access context, and any requested output limit.
Captured inputs flow to workers; findings return with evidence references and uncertainty.
Saved records carry completion status and input identity into browser, CLI, HTTP, MCP, and portable outputs.
Freshness reports describe a check at a stated time. They cannot promise that a repository remains unchanged afterward.
operating_model: Run one controller and a bounded worker pool. Keep these responsibilities in one installable application.
Use saved request identifiers to retrieve progress after a caller disconnects.
Inspect queue depth, worker failures, save failures, and input-change reports when diagnosing incomplete work.
Validate backups before confirmed restore and report whether recovery completed.
Choose worker and storage limits from measured workloads; the supplied scope gives no general performance promise.

relationships.rationale: Every analysis entry point applies the same configured access rules.
The controller receives resolved targets and permitted actions.
The controller knows whether usable inputs exist before starting analysis.
One owner decides worker limits, cancellation, and attempt validity.
A running analysis reads a stable set of permitted inputs.
Workers cannot independently declare a request complete.
Progress and accepted findings stay consistent.
Saved findings remain tied to the inputs that produced them.
All response forms use the same saved findings and outcomes.
A later read can disclose changes since analysis.
Each interface translates one shared outcome into its own response form.
Restore cannot race with active request updates.
Confirmed recovery replaces saved state only after active work has stopped.

design.state_ownership: The controller alone changes request progress and accepts worker findings. The record store owns saved records. Input capture owns captured repository content and its fingerprints. Workers own temporary calculations. Entry points and formatters hold only request-local state. Restore runs while request processing is stopped.
design.summary: Use one service with a saved record for each analysis request. A single controller owns request progress and starts bounded worker processes. Workers read captured repository inputs and return findings with evidence. All user interfaces share access checks and result rules. This design makes cancellation, stale inputs, partial results, and worker failure explicit without adding an event service.

value_json.summary: The supplied assessment holds up. A transactional inbox saves the ID of each received message in the same database write as the changes that message causes. That way, a repeated message cannot repeat the changes. The best place to check for this need is agent-result submission. Agents claim jobs with lease tokens (temporary permission slips) and send results back. A sent result could be sent again if the first reply was lost. value_json.summary: The assessment holds up against the supplied evidence. AnaxiGraph has a simple /healthz check that answers {"status":"ok"} and a more detailed /api/health report. value_json.rationale: A circuit breaker pauses calls after repeated dependency failures, then allows limited calls to check recovery. The strongest case here is a shared provider outage that makes many jobs wait for the same failure. The strongest case against it is that bad requests and invalid outputs can fail independently; pausing the provider would then reject useful work. Keep the current behavior until failure records distinguish these cases. If failures are isolated, bounded retries with increasing delays are simpler.

A short pause could cause repeated bursts; a long pause could delay recovery.
Separate counters in each worker could allow more recovery calls than intended.

issues.explanation: In the supplied code, start_fresh_eyes and prepare both call asyncio.to_thread. That Python function sends work to the event loop's one default thread pool, so these two jobs share the same workers. Plain 'def' routes such as status and findings are run by FastAPI in a different thread pool. So short status reads may already be partly kept apart from expensive planning work by accident. The assessment says short requests and expensive work may share scarce workers, but it does not mention this split that already exists.

design.control_model: A build request goes: pin a scan, group responsibilities, check, save, then assess, check, save. Assessment starts only after grouping has saved its claims for that scan and method. A read request goes: pin a scan, read the claim book, add the newer-scan notice, build the output, and tag the reply. If claims for that scan and method are missing, the read returns 'not built yet' rather than starting a build silently. Building and reading are separate requests so a slow build never blocks reading older results.
extension_strategy: Add a new output kind, such as a change-impact note, by adding a new way to build output from existing claims.
Add a new review rule as a new assessment method version. Old judgments stay readable beside new ones.
Add a new grouping method by giving it a new method version. Readers can compare methods on the same scan.
design.failure_isolation: A grouping or assessment run that fails adds a 'stopped early' marker. Claims already saved remain readable and are labeled incomplete. A claim with a broken evidence link is rejected alone and does not block the others. A failed output build loses nothing, because nothing is saved there. If s04 cannot be reached, the newer-scan notice says 'could not check' and output still appears. A shared claim-book failure stops new builds for every repository. This design does not isolate that.

design.state_ownership: s04 owns scans, source structure, and relationships. This capability never copies or changes them; it stores only links into them. The claim book owns all claims and judgments, filed by scan and method version. Grouping and assessment hold only temporary working data during one run. The output builder, newer-scan notice, and reply guard save nothing. Each reader's current selection belongs to that reader's interface.
design.summary: Every statement this capability makes is saved once as a claim. A claim is one short statement, such as 'this group of files handles login', plus links to the evidence behind it and a note on how sure it is. Each claim is tied to one saved scan from s04. Explanations, responsibility maps, and architecture reviews are not saved as separate documents. They are built on request from the claims. A review judgment, such as 'this part mixes two jobs', must point to the claims it relies on. So every sentence a reader sees can be traced back to evidence, and all three outputs agree because they read the same claims.

parent_constraints: The parent must apply repository and MCP profile access checks before any scan is pinned or claims are returned.
The parent must provide a saved-record area that adds entries without editing them, or must let the claim book own its own entries.
The parent must carry selection tags or request identifiers so late replies can be dropped.

pros: Explanations, maps, and reviews cannot contradict each other, because all three are built from the same saved claims.
Every review judgment points to claims, and every claim points to scan evidence. Readers and agents can check why a statement was made.
Old claims are never edited. A reader can compare what was said about an older scan with what is said about a newer one.
Saving nothing at the output step means a formatting failure loses no work.
